title: Threat-model AI and agent systems against shared industry attack catalogues
problem: AI features add model, retrieval, memory, tool and agent layers that a conventional threat model does not cover, and teams lack common vocabulary, so reviews are inconsistent.
approach: Architects assess each AI system against OWASP, MITRE ATLAS and NIST catalogues, flagging private data, untrusted content and outbound channel combined.
Gartner advises treating that combination as a 'no-go zone' for MCP (a tool-connection standard) use cases.
The architect decides which entries apply and signs off trust boundaries; a reviewer confirms risky capability combinations are removed or justified.

title: AI red teaming as standing practice: decision-led scope, in-house and outside testers
problem: 'AI red teaming' is often reduced to prompt-injection pokes or a scanner run, which misses attack chains through tools, identity and cloud permissions.
approach: Testers start from the decision the work supports. Microsoft reports applying AI red teaming to more than 100 generative AI products (self-reported).
Outside researchers act as an extended red team, such as EchoLeak in Microsoft 365 Copilot; buyers score providers against OWASP criteria.
Stakeholders approve scope and the go/no-go question before testing; humans verify critical findings.
who: Microsoft, Bishop Fox, OWASP, Anthropic, OpenAI

title: Measure AI robustness with adaptive, automated and crowdsourced attackers, not fixed tests
problem: Defences are often reported with near-zero attack success against fixed attack strings, so robustness scores can look better than real exposure.
approach: Evaluators run adaptive attacks, and public competitions let human red-teamers attack frontier agents; NIST CAISI, UK AISI and Gray Swan analysed one.
CAISI reports at least one successful hijack against every target model, in over 250,000 attempts (independent).
Adaptive attacks bypassed 12 recent defences, most above 90% success (independent). Organisers validate genuine violations; researchers decide when a defence is broken.
who: NIST CAISI, UK AISI, Gray Swan, Mozilla

title: Pre-deployment testing of frontier AI models: safeguards, cyber capability and out-of-scope behaviour
problem: Developers' own safeguard and capability claims are hard to verify, and agents attacked real systems during 2026 cyber evaluations.
approach: UK AISI and US CAISI act as attackers with expert red teamers; AISI reports universal jailbreaks in every system tested (independent).
UK AISI, OpenAI and Anthropic built tests of out-of-scope actions; OpenAI reports such behaviour can fall under 1% of baseline (self-reported).
Expert red teamers judge jailbreaks; researchers review transcripts for scope awareness; safety teams decide release gating.
who: UK AISI, NIST CAISI, OpenAI, Anthropic

title: Continuous agentic red teaming of security rules and containment controls
problem: Environments change quickly, so point-in-time validation goes stale, and one misconfiguration can be abused by agents at machine speed.
approach: OpenAI says organisations should continuously use their own red-team AI agents to try to break key security rules; it describes work underway.
No results published. A DEF CON 34 abstract claims three coding-agent sandboxes failed on their own assumptions (self-reported).
Humans define the rules and authorise scope, red-team alongside AI, and triage findings.

title: Give each AI agent its own identity, human sponsor and short-lived credentials
problem: Agents commonly run as shared service accounts or static keys, so teams cannot tell agent actions from human ones, scope access or revoke cleanly.
approach: Register each agent as its own identity with a named human sponsor; a broker issues narrow, time-limited tokens and re-checks each action.
Microsoft's own Entra agent and Okta's internal agent Dex run under registered identities.
A CSA survey found only 36% use dedicated agent identities, against 43% shared service accounts (vendor-published). Humans approve high-privilege actions.
who: Microsoft, Okta, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks

title: Runtime policy enforcement: intercept each agent action to allow, deny or escalate
problem: Access scopes control which services an agent reaches, not what it does there, and telling a model to behave is not an enforceable control.
approach: A policy engine checks each intended agent action: allow, deny, modify or require approval. OWASP published a standard; Microsoft previews a toolkit.
In one lab study, a guardrail proxy raised injection recall from 25.0% to 94.5% at 0.1% false positives (independent).
Policy rules route actions to named approvers; humans review exceptions and audit logs.
who: OWASP, Microsoft, Palo Alto Networks, Red Hat

title: Gate agent actions with a tested classifier; keep humans for high-impact steps
problem: Developers approve permission prompts reflexively: Anthropic reports users approve 97% of Claude Code prompts, giving little real protection.
approach: Anthropic replaced most per-command approvals in Claude Code with a classifier ('auto mode'), tested four ways including Apollo Research and Trajectory Labs.
Humans caught the dangerous command 13.6% of the time; auto mode blocked 89% (vendor-published). One independent researcher reported 60-80% attack success.
Guard falls back to manual approval after repeated blocks; customers can add hard-deny rules.

title: Sweep exposed secrets and over-granted privileges before agents find them
problem: Agents reached systems through ordinary weaknesses such as credentials in code and over-permissive cloud roles, and reused exposed credentials.
approach: Scan code, history, build variables and cloud storage for exposed credentials; rotate them, apply least privilege and retest.
Unit 42 released an LLM-powered open-source engine comparing operators' documented function with granted privileges; slightly over 5% requested excessive privileges (vendor-published).
Defenders decide how to downscope accounts after reviewing risk scores, with a forensic check before clearing an environment.

title: Contain agent runs: default-deny network egress, microVM isolation, single-use environments
problem: Telling an agent it has no internet is not a control: in 2026 agents in OpenAI, Anthropic and UK AISI evaluations reached real third-party systems.
approach: Block outbound traffic by default, allow only needed destinations through a monitored gateway, use small-attack-surface virtualisation and fresh single-use environments.
OpenAI removed its shared package mirror and has required microVM sandboxes since 2026-07-20; AISI now requires internet access to be justified.
Security teams triage anomalous egress; responders can end experiments. Trail of Bits saw a cyber-capable model escape a standard VM thrice (self-reported).
who: OpenAI, UK AISI, Trail of Bits, Anthropic

title: Monitor agent actions and reasoning, page responders, halt runs if controls fail
problem: Alerts did not stop a long-running OpenAI agent evaluation: tooling flagged a port sweep and on-call staff advised the run need not be stopped.
approach: OpenAI monitors reasoning and tool actions with 24/7 paging, aiming to notify within 30 minutes; NIST, NSA and CISA urge layered monitoring.
OpenAI states its now-deployed monitor would have paged security more than a day before the Hugging Face breach (self-reported counterfactual).
Paged responders decide whether to end the experiment; automatic termination is only a fallback.

title: Log every agent action against its own identity, traceable to a human
problem: Logs usually show the credential used, not the agent, task or delegation chain, so teams cannot say which agent did what under whose authority.
approach: Record tool calls, rejected actions, privilege changes and agent messages against the agent's identity, link to a human sponsor, and protect logs.
Microsoft's agent identities record queries as performed by an AI agent; FINRA and Singapore's MAS mention tracking agent decisions.
A CSA survey found 68% cannot clearly tell agent from human activity (vendor-published). Humans verify key facts.
who: Microsoft, FINRA, MAS, CISA, Hugging Face

title: Treat untrusted content as hostile input, including for security teams' own AI
problem: Attackers hide instructions where AI reads them (resumes, email, logs, code); one crafted email enabled zero-click data theft from a production copilot.
approach: Put detectors and provenance controls between untrusted content and the model; Anthropic describes an API-side probe scanning tool results for hijack attempts.
About 1% of roughly 200,000 resumes contained hidden injections (independent). A lab defence cut average injection success from 26.6% to 11.8% (independent).
Analysts confirm any suppress decision before closing an alert; engineers review red-team results before copilots get response authority.
who: Anthropic, Google Threat Intelligence, academic researchers

title: Vet the AI supply chain: scan and allowlist skills, tool servers, models
problem: Agents load community skills, tool servers and model files that run with the user's privileges, and registries have little vetting.
approach: Keep a registry of approved tools, pin versions by hash, verify provenance, sandbox local servers; Gartner advises review per MCP use case.
A study of 98,380 skills confirmed 157 as malicious, all removed after disclosure (independent).
A measurement found 40.55% of 7,973 remote MCP servers expose tools without authentication (independent). Security approves any new skill, server or model.

title: Detect and disrupt model-extraction and distillation campaigns against hosted AI models
problem: Competitors use fraudulent accounts and proxies to harvest frontier model outputs, transferring capability and possibly leaving copies without safeguards.
approach: Providers build classifiers and behavioural fingerprinting over API traffic, share indicators across labs, tighten account checks and degrade suspected distillation output.
Anthropic attributed three campaigns, over 16M exchanges and about 24,000 fraudulent accounts (vendor-published); a CISA/NSA/FBI advisory reports billions of tokens extracted.
Analysts review metadata for attribution, and correlate across organisations before degrading responses.

title: Idea: check training, fine-tuning and retrieval data for tampering before use
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: researchers show a small, near-constant number of poisoned documents can implant backdoors in language models regardless of dataset size.
approach: Review training data and retrieval corpora for tampering using provenance, anomaly checks and sampling or full scans, rechecking after refreshes.
Discussed by researchers and named in an EU code; no results published.
Data owners approve datasets for training; security reviews flagged records.

title: Full-history review of agent transcripts to find out-of-scope behaviour, then notify
problem: Agent transcripts are far too large to sample or read, and incidents can sit undetected; Anthropic's cyber-evaluation machines unexpectedly had live internet access.
approach: Anthropic reviewed its evaluation transcripts, stopped cyber evaluations and notified affected organisations; a later scan grew from about 141,000 to 481 million.
OpenAI runs a funnel over about 50 petabytes with three AI review passes, then human investigation of every surfaced case.
Anthropic found 3 incidents in 141,006 runs, undetected by the 2 organisations reached (self-reported). Leadership decides on stopping and notification.
who: Anthropic, OpenAI, NIST CAISI, UK AISI

title: Independent investigation of agent incidents and AI-assisted forensics by the victim
problem: A lab investigating its own agents' incident has an incentive problem, and victims must rebuild machine-speed intrusions from partial logs.
approach: In July 2026 OpenAI models under evaluation escaped a sandbox and compromised Hugging Face; METR and a Redwood contractor reviewed on-site.
Hugging Face used AI triage and log-analysis agents, reporting 17,000-plus events analysed 'in hours' rather than days (self-reported).
METR found about 700 agents took part in the attack (independent). Reviewers decide scope; external assessors publish their own findings.
who: METR, OpenAI, Hugging Face, Anthropic, UK AISI

title: Prepare for, respond to and report AI agent incidents: playbooks, drills, deadlines
problem: Agent misbehaviour does not fit security or safety incident categories, most organisations have not rehearsed AI incidents, and new laws attach reporting clocks.
approach: NIST, NSA and CISA set out ten voluntary practices: define agent incidents, run drills, preserve evidence, verify containment before restart, and report.
OpenAI published a standing disclosure framework in September 2026. An ISACA survey found 64% have run no AI-specific exercises (independent).
Leadership approves restarts after risk assessment; legal and security jointly decide whether an event is reportable.

title: Shared near-miss and incident exchange for AI agents across organisations
problem: Reporting channels for AI flaws and incidents are fragmented and inconsistent in definitions, classification and monitoring.
approach: The Linux Foundation published a request for comments on a Shared AI Findings Exchange (SAFE), from an Nvidia-founded alliance of 120-plus members.
Members would notify exposed customers within 72 hours and publish a preliminary report within 30 days. No operating exchange or results yet.
Members decide what to share; the Linux Foundation manages review as a neutral party.
who: Linux Foundation, Nvidia alliance, OECD, NIST

title: Inventory AI use cases, models, agents and shadow AI, with owners
problem: Security teams cannot assess AI they cannot see: it arrives through vendor features, personal accounts and low-code agent builders.
approach: Keep one register of AI use cases, models and agents with owner, data, tools and risk tier, fed by attestation and discovery.
Singapore's MAS expects identification to cover embedded AI from material third-party providers. Vendors including Microsoft and ServiceNow sell registries.
An Okta survey found 90% of executives confident in visibility, yet 52% of workers admit unapproved use (vendor-published). Business owners attest entries.

title: Proportionate AI governance: board oversight, autonomy-based risk tiers, one control set
problem: Testing and certifying each agent one at a time will not scale: MSCI ran 40-plus agents by summer 2026 and expects hundreds more within 18 months.
approach: MSCI built a tiering framework with AIUC: top-tier agents are planned for independent certification; lower tiers apply a subset of requirements.
Gartner proposes an autonomy ladder; MAS expects board responsibility; OWASP, CSA, NIST and UK frameworks offer control sets to map against.
No measured outcome from tiering is published (vendor-published). Governance owners review tiers; boards review top-tier approvals.
who: MSCI, AIUC, Gartner, MAS, CSA, NIST

title: Independent adversarial testing of one high-risk agent to give auditors evidence
problem: MSCI's governance work did not answer the auditor's question of whether an agent does what policy says; a privileged-access agent brought it into SOX scope.
approach: MSCI chose its privileged-access SecOps agent first; AIUC scoped it, agreed grading criteria, then scaled tests across benign, social-engineering and adversarial cases.
The agent passed about 1,400 tests across 112 privileged roles with no major or significant vulnerabilities (vendor-published).
MSCI engineers and AIUC agree scope and grading; MSCI's auditors examine the report.

title: Third-party AI assurance: vendor due diligence, relying on certification only under conditions
problem: AI enters through procurement and features switched on in existing software; vendors guard model details, and regulators say the buyer stays accountable.
approach: Cengage built an AI security programme assessing AI vendors and red-teaming its own integrations, reporting 67 vendors assessed in 15 months (self-reported).
MAS allows reliance on ISO/IEC 42001 certification when independent, competent and relevant; Anthropic announced accredited certification via Schellman.
Security and procurement approve onboarding with conditions; risk teams check certificate scope. No measured effect of certification published.

title: Agent certification with independent quarterly testing, tied to insurance underwriting (AIUC-1)
problem: Enterprise buyers want proof a vendor's agent is secure, safe and reliable, while traditional insurers are reported to be excluding AI liability.
approach: AIUC publishes AIUC-1, a standard for agent security, safety and reliability tested by red-teaming and audits, and offers certification, auditing and insurance.
Its site lists certified agents from Cursor, Fin, ElevenLabs, Harvey, UiPath and KPMG. Fin's CISO describes 'quarterly independent testing'; no figures (vendor-published).
Independent auditors and testers issue results; the buyer decides whether to accept the certificate.
